title: Frog — Digestive, Circulatory and Respiratory Systems
topicTitle: Frog: Blood vascular system (structure and working mechanism of heart); respiratory system (respiratory organs and physiology of respiration)
notes: **Digestive organs:** mouth → buccal cavity (tongue, vomerine teeth, maxillary teeth) → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach (pepsin, HCl) → duodenum (bile and pancreatic ducts) → ileum (absorption, villi) → large intestine (water absorption) → cloaca.

**Heart:** three-chambered: two auricles + one ventricle. Right auricle receives deoxygenated blood from body; left auricle receives oxygenated blood from lungs and skin. Single ventricle pumps mixed blood to body and lungs.

**Working mechanism:** deoxygenated blood enters right auricle via superior/inferior vena cava; oxygenated blood enters left auricle via pulmonary veins. Both auricles contract simultaneously, pushing blood into ventricle. Spiral valve in conus arteriosus directs deoxygenated blood to pulmocutaneous arches and oxygenated blood to systemic arches.
**Respiratory organs:** skin (cutaneous respiration, highly vascularised, moist), buccal cavity, lungs (simple sacs with internal alveoli).

**Respiration physiology:** on land, lungs inflate by buccal pumping (lower floor of buccal cavity draws air in, then close nostrils and raise floor forcing air into lungs). Skin respiration always active in moist environment.

**Teeth in frog:** frog has two types of teeth in the upper jaw only — maxillary teeth (small, along the upper jaw margin, for gripping prey) and vomerine teeth (two small patches on the roof of the buccal cavity, between the internal nostrils). There are NO lower jaw teeth. Teeth are not used for chewing but only for holding food so the tongue can push it into the pharynx.

**Digestion process:** in the stomach, gastric glands secrete HCl (creates acidic pH ~2) and pepsinogen which is activated to pepsin for protein digestion. The stomach churns food mechanically. Semi-digested food (chyme) passes into the duodenum where bile from the liver (emulsifies fats) and pancreatic juice (contains lipase, trypsin, amylase for fat, protein, and carbohydrate digestion respectively) are secreted.

**Absorption:** the ileum has villi and microvilli that increase surface area for absorption of nutrients into blood capillaries. Water and remaining nutrients are absorbed in the large intestine. Undigested waste is expelled through the cloaca.

**Liver and pancreas:** liver is the largest gland, producing bile (stored in gall bladder) which has no digestive enzyme but emulsifies large fat globules into smaller ones. Pancreas is both exocrine (secretes digestive enzymes into duodenum via pancreatic duct) and endocrine (islets of Langerhans secrete insulin and glucagon for blood sugar regulation).

**Double circulation in frog:** blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit — pulmonary circulation (heart → lungs/skin → heart) and systemic circulation (heart → body → heart). This is less efficient than the complete double circulation of birds and mammals because of some mixing in the single ventricle.

**Arterial system:** from the ventricle, three pairs of arterial arches arise — (1) carotid arches (supply oxygenated blood to head and brain), (2) systemic arches (supply mixed blood to the body, curves dorsally and joins to form dorsal aorta), (3) pulmocutaneous arches (carry deoxygenated blood to lungs and skin for oxygenation).

**Venous system:** deoxygenated blood returns via two main veins — anterior (superior) vena cava from head and forelimbs, and posterior (inferior) vena cava from trunk, hindlimbs, and kidneys. Both open into the sinus venosus which drains into the right auricle. Hepatic portal system carries blood from intestine to liver for processing.

**Spiral valve function:** the conus arteriosus contains a spiral valve that partially divides the ventricle and directs blood flow. During ventricular contraction, deoxygenated blood is preferentially directed towards the pulmocutaneous arches while oxygenated blood is directed towards systemic and carotid arches. This minimises mixing despite the single ventricle.

**Buccal respiration mechanism:** the frog uses positive pressure breathing (unlike mammals which use negative pressure). The nostrils open, the floor of the buccal cavity drops drawing air in through the nostrils (buccal inflation). Then nostrils close, the floor rises, and the glottis opens forcing air into the lungs (lung inflation). This buccal pumping is repeated several times for ventilation.

**Cardiac cycle and electrical conduction — the frog heart is myogenic (self-exciting). The sinus venosus acts as the natural pacemaker, initiating each heartbeat. The impulse spreads across the auricles (via Purkinje-like fibres), causing auricular systole, then travels through the atrioventricular node (AV node) to the ventricle, causing ventricular systole. There is a brief delay at the AV node, ensuring auricles contract before the ventricle.

**Sinus venosus structure and function — the sinus venosus is a thin-walled sac that receives deoxygenated blood from the two vena cavae and the coronary sinus (from heart muscle). Its wall contains specialised pacemaker cells with automaticity. This structure is homologous to the sinoatrial (SA) node in mammals, demonstrating evolutionary continuity in cardiac pacemaking.

**Conus arteriosus and spiral valve morphology — the conus arteriosus is a muscular tube extending from the ventricle into the truncus arteriosus. Its lumen contains the spiral valve, a corkscrew-shaped muscular flap that spirals around the interior. During systole, the spiral valve's orientation guides deoxygenated blood (from the right side of the ventricle) into the pulmocutaneous arches and oxygenated blood (from the left side) into the systemic and carotid arches, achieving partial separation.

**Coronary circulation in frog — the heart muscle itself receives oxygenated blood via the coronary arteries that branch from the systemic arches. The coronary sinus returns deoxygenated blood directly to the sinus venosus. This arrangement ensures the working myocardium receives high-oxygen blood, especially important given the mixing in the ventricle.

**Cutaneous respiration ultrastructure — the skin's epidermis is thin (2–3 cell layers) and richly vascularised with capillaries that extend into the dermal papillae. The diffusion distance for O₂ and CO₂ is extremely short (~5–10 μm). The skin surface has a network of mucous glands whose secretions maintain a thin water film, enabling gas dissolution and diffusion even on land.

**Buccal respiration anatomy — the buccal cavity floor is muscular (buccinator and hyoid muscles) and highly vascularised. During buccal respiration, the glottis remains closed and the nostrils open/close rhythmically. The vascularised lining of the buccal cavity exchanges gases directly with the air, supplementing lung ventilation and serving as a primary respiratory surface in tadpoles.

**Lung internal structure — frog lungs are simple, thin-walled sacs (not alveolated like mammalian lungs). The inner surface has a honeycomb of low ridges (faveoli) that increase surface area slightly. The lungs are poorly vascularised compared to mammals, reflecting their secondary role. Ventilation is by buccal pumping, not diaphragmatic action.

**Renal portal system — deoxygenated blood from the hindlimbs enters the renal portal vein, passes through the kidney's capillary network (where additional filtration occurs), and then joins the posterior vena cava. This system allows the kidneys to filter metabolic waste from the hindlimb circulation before it returns to the heart, a unique feature in amphibians and reptiles.

**Hepatic portal system in digestion — blood from the stomach, intestine, and spleen drains via the hepatic portal vein into the liver sinusoids. Here, nutrients are absorbed, toxins detoxified, and glucose stored as glycogen or released. The hepatic vein then carries processed blood to the sinus venosus. This system is critical for maintaining metabolic homeostasis after feeding.

**Vagal control of heart rate — the vagus nerve (parasympathetic) innervates the sinus venosus and AV node, slowing heart rate. In resting frogs, vagal tone is high, producing a slow heart rate (~30–40 bpm). During exercise or stress, sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate to ~60–80 bpm. This autonomic control is conserved across vertebrates.

**CO₂ transport in frog blood — CO₂ is transported in three forms: dissolved in plasma (~10%), as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) after conversion by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs (~70%), and as carbamino compounds bound to haemoglobin (~20%). The Bohr effect (pH-dependent O₂ binding) and Haldane effect (O₂-dependent CO₂ binding) operate in frog blood, facilitating gas exchange at both tissues and respiratory surfaces.

**Temperature effects on frog circulation — as ectotherms, frogs' heart rate and blood pressure vary with environmental temperature (Q₁₀ ~2–3). At 10°C, heart rate may drop to 15 bpm; at 25°C, it rises to 50–60 bpm. The spiral valve's efficiency in separating blood streams also varies with temperature, affecting oxygen delivery efficiency across seasons.

**Metabolic switching during hibernation — during winter hibernation (in mud at pond bottom), frogs shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism. The heart continues to beat slowly (~5–10 bpm) using cutaneous O₂. Glycogen stores in the liver and muscle are mobilised. Lactate accumulates but is buffered by the alkaline urine and bone carbonate. Thyroid hormone levels drop, reducing basal metabolic rate by ~90%.
confusion: Frog's heart is three-chambered (2 auricles + 1 ventricle) — do NOT say it is two-chambered like a fish. Fish have two chambers (1 auricle + 1 ventricle). Frog has an additional left auricle for receiving oxygenated blood.

The spiral valve in the conus arteriosus helps minimise mixing of blood in the ventricle, but some mixing STILL occurs. This is why frog circulation is called 'incompletely double' — not perfectly efficient like the four-chambered heart of mammals.
Frog uses POSITIVE pressure breathing (buccal pumping pushes air into lungs) — mammals use NEGATIVE pressure breathing (diaphragm creates vacuum to pull air in). Do not confuse the two mechanisms.

Cutaneous (skin) respiration is NOT a backup system — it is always active and contributes significantly to gas exchange, especially during hibernation in water when the frog stops using lungs entirely.
The bile produced by the liver does NOT contain digestive enzymes — it only emulsifies (breaks into smaller droplets) fats mechanically. Enzymatic fat digestion is done by lipase from the pancreas.

Confusing the conus arteriosus with the truncus arteriosus — Correct explanation: the conus arteriosus is the proximal, muscular portion of the outflow tract that contains the spiral valve. The truncus arteriosus is the distal, non-muscular portion that divides into the three arterial arches. They are distinct segments with different functions.

Thinking the spiral valve completely separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood — Correct explanation: the spiral valve only PARTIALLY separates the blood streams. Because the ventricle is a single chamber, some mixing always occurs. The spiral valve minimises but does not eliminate mixing, which is why frog circulation is called 'incomplete double circulation'.

Assuming the frog's lungs are the primary respiratory organ — Correct explanation: in adult frogs at rest, cutaneous respiration can account for 30–50% of total gas exchange, and buccal respiration another 20–30%. The lungs are used mainly during activity. Only during vigorous exercise do lungs become the dominant respiratory surface.

Believing the frog's bile is stored in the gallbladder like mammals — Correct explanation: the frog's gallbladder is a small, thin-walled sac embedded in the liver, but it is often poorly developed or absent in some species. Bile flows continuously from the liver into the duodenum via the common bile duct, with less reliance on storage compared to mammals.

Confusing the renal portal system with the hepatic portal system — Correct explanation: the HEPATIC portal system carries blood from the DIGESTIVE TRACT to the liver for nutrient processing. The RENAL portal system carries blood from the HINDLIMBS through the KIDNEYS for filtration before returning to the heart. They serve completely different organs and functions.

Misconceiving the AV node delay as a defect — Correct explanation: the brief pause at the atrioventricular (AV) node is ESSENTIAL — it allows the auricles to finish contracting and emptying their blood into the ventricle before the ventricle contracts. Without this delay, the ventricle would contract prematurely, reducing cardiac output. This is a feature, not a bug, conserved in all vertebrate hearts.

Thinking frog RBCs lack a nucleus like mammals — Correct explanation: frog red blood cells are NUCLEATED (oval, nucleated cells). The nucleus occupies much of the cell volume, reducing haemoglobin content per cell compared to mammalian enucleated RBCs. This is the ancestral vertebrate condition; enucleated RBCs evolved later in mammals and birds.

Assuming the frog heart lacks a pacemaker — Correct explanation: the sinus venosus IS the natural pacemaker, containing specialised myogenic cells that spontaneously depolarise. It is homologous to the SA node in mammals. Experiments show that if the sinus venosus is removed, the AV node takes over as a slower backup pacemaker.

universalFacts: The frog's stomach pH can drop to about 1.5–2.0 due to HCl secretion, which is comparable to the stomach pH of carnivorous mammals and is essential for activating pepsin.
Frog blood contains nucleated red blood cells (erythrocytes), unlike mammals which have enucleated RBCs. The nucleus in frog RBCs means they carry less haemoglobin per cell.

The hepatic portal system in frogs is homologous to that in mammals — blood from the digestive tract passes through the liver before entering general circulation, allowing detoxification and nutrient processing.
During hibernation, a frog's metabolic rate drops by up to 90%, and it relies almost entirely on cutaneous respiration through the skin while submerged in water or buried in mud.

The three arterial arches (carotid, systemic, pulmocutaneous) are evolutionarily significant — they represent the ancestral condition from which the different arterial systems of reptiles, birds, and mammals evolved.

The frog's sinus venosus pacemaker cells exhibit spontaneous depolarisation due to a 'funny current' (I_f) — an inward Na⁺/K⁺ current activated by hyperpolarisation, the same mechanism found in the mammalian SA node, demonstrating deep evolutionary conservation of cardiac pacemaking.

Frog haemoglobin has a lower O₂ affinity (P₅₀ ~25–30 mmHg) than mammalian haemoglobin, facilitating O₂ release to tissues at the lower partial pressures typical of ectothermic vertebrates with mixed circulation.

The frog's conus arteriosus contains 3–4 complete turns of the spiral valve, and the angle of the spiral correlates with the degree of blood stream separation — a steeper spiral achieves better separation, representing an evolutionary optimisation.

Frog blood contains thrombocytes (nucleated platelets) rather than anucleate platelets. Thrombocytes are larger, have a nucleus, and participate in both clotting and immune responses, representing the ancestral vertebrate condition.

The hepatic portal vein in frogs receives blood not only from the digestive organs but also from the spleen, making it a 'splenomesenteric' portal system. This allows the liver to filter both dietary nutrients and splenic immune products before they enter systemic circulation.

Carbonic anhydrase activity in frog RBCs is among the highest measured in vertebrates, enabling rapid CO₂ ↔ HCO₃⁻ interconversion during the brief capillary transit time in cutaneous and pulmonary capillaries.

The frog's heart can continue beating for hours after excision if kept in oxygenated Ringer's solution, demonstrating its strong myogenic property. This made it a classic preparation for early cardiac physiology studies by Starling and others.

The renal portal system in frogs allows the kidneys to extract urea and other wastes directly from hindlimb blood before it returns to the heart, providing an extra filtration step that conserves water during terrestrial life.

Frog lung surfactant is compositionally simpler than mammalian surfactant, containing mostly phosphatidylcholine with fewer hydrophobic proteins. This reflects the simpler alveolar structure and lower surface tension requirements of frog lungs.

The frog's intestinal villi are shorter and less branched than mammalian villi, but the microvilli are densely packed. This provides adequate absorption surface for the rapid transit time typical of carnivorous digestion.

Vagal stimulation of the frog heart causes a negative chronotropic effect via acetylcholine binding to muscarinic M₂ receptors on sinus venosus cells, opening K⁺ channels and hyperpolarising the membrane — the same mechanism as in mammals.
